name: Roman Empire
peak: Under Trajan (117 AD) it stretched from Britain to the Persian Gulf, the largest empire the west had ever seen, connected by 80,000 km of roads.
rise: Born from the Roman Republic's civil wars, Octavian became Augustus in 27 BC and built an empire of law, legions and aqueducts. Rome swallowed Carthage, Greece, Gaul and Egypt, then ruled the Mediterranean as 'our sea', Mare Nostrum.
fall: Divided and attacked from every side, the Western Empire buckled as Goths, Vandals and Huns poured across the borders. In 476 the German general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, a painfully poetic ending.
legacy: Roman law, Latin (the root of French, Spanish, Italian and more), Christianity's spread, and the very idea of Europe still carry the Roman imprint.
quizFact: The smallest Roman coins were so small that people sometimes lost them between floor tiles, and archaeologists still find them.
builder: Augustus (Octavian), heir of Julius Caesar, after decades of civil war.
reach: About 5 million km2 at its height under Trajan: Britain to the Persian Gulf, the Rhine to the Sahara, roughly 60-70 million people.
darkSide: Conquest meant enslavement on an industrial scale - Gaul lost perhaps a third of its population in Caesar's campaigns, and Carthage was erased so completely the fields were salted by legend. Crucifixion, arena executions and mass slave markets were the machinery of empire; emperors were betrayed by their own guards more often than by foreign foes - Caligula, Claudius and Gaius all died by palace knives.
deepLore: Rome's genius was turning enemies into stakeholders: conquered elites could become citizens, senators, even emperors from Spain, Africa and the Balkans. The legions built roads, aqueducts and cities that outlived the empire by millennia. But the Pretorian Guard - created to protect the emperor - became his most frequent assassins, auctioning the throne in 193 AD. When Diocletian split administration and Constantine moved the capital east to Byzantium, the western half was left to pay for its own defense; within 80 years it hired the very barbarians who buried it.

name: Byzantine Empire
peak: Justinian's generals reconquered Italy and North Africa in the 530s, and Hagia Sophia's dome awed the world.
rise: When Rome's west collapsed, the eastern half survived with its capital on the Bosphorus. The Byzantines called themselves Romans, preserved Greek and Roman learning, and made Orthodox Christianity the empire's soul.
fall: Squeezed for centuries by Crusaders (who sacked Constantinople in 1204) and then the rising Ottomans, the empire shrank to a city-state. On 29 May 1453 Sultan Mehmed II's army breached the walls with massive cannons, and Emperor Constantine XI died fighting in the breach.
legacy: Orthodox Christianity, Greek manuscripts preserved for posterity, and legal code that underpins much of European law.
quizFact: Greek fire, a burning weapon that even ignited on water, was a Byzantine state secret so protected its formula is still unknown.
builder: Constantine the Great, refounding Byzantium as New Rome in 330 AD.
reach: At its peak under Justinian it reclaimed Italy, North Africa and southern Spain - about 2.8 million km2 - and it held Asia Minor and the Balkans for most of a millennium.
darkSide: Court intrigue was a blood sport: emperors were blinded, castrated or strangled by uncles, wives and generals - Basil I murdered his patron Michael III to take the throne. The Fourth Crusade of 1204, aimed at Jerusalem, was diverted to Constantinople by Venetian money and a betrayed claimant; the city was raped and looted for three days by fellow Christians. Religious dissenters suffered persecution, most famously the Iconoclast purges.
deepLore: Byzantium survived 1,123 years by diplomacy as much as war - the 'Byzantine' playbook of marriage alliances, bribes, hostages and playing enemies against each other is literally the word for scheming today. It preserved Greek and Roman texts that would later ignite the Renaissance. Greek fire guarded the Bosporus for seven centuries until the secret died with the empire. In the end, cannon ended what Attila and the Avars could not: on the last day, 29 May 1453, the emperor removed his imperial insignia and died unrecognized in the breach.

name: Macedonian Empire (Alexander the Great)
peak: Alexander's empire ran from Greece to the Indus River, the largest the world had seen by age 25.
rise: King Philip II forged Macedonia's army into a phalanx machine; his son Alexander, tutored by Aristotle, destroyed the Persian Empire in a decade of lightning campaigns.
fall: Alexander died of fever in Babylon at just 32 with no clear heir. His generals tore the empire apart in 40 years of civil war, carving it into dynasties like the Ptolemies of Egypt and the Seleucids of Asia.
legacy: Hellenistic culture fusing Greek and Asian worlds; cities named Alexandria dot the map from Egypt to Central Asia.
quizFact: Alexander named over 20 cities after himself, and only one, Alexandria in Egypt, kept the name.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
peak: Under Darius I it ruled ~44% of humankind, the largest empire of the ancient world, linked by the Royal Road.
rise: Cyrus the Great rebelled against the Medes, then conquered Babylon with a policy of tolerance that freed the Jews of exile. His dynasty built an administration of satraps, coinage and roads that ran from Greece to India.
fall: Persia spent 150 years clashing with Greek city-states, then fell to Alexander the Great, who burned Persepolis in 330 BC after three decisive battles.
legacy: Zoroastrian ideas, imperial administration models, and the Cyrus Cylinder's early declaration of human rights.
quizFact: The Royal Road from Susa to Sardis stretched 2,700 km, and a royal messenger could cross it in seven days using relay stations.

name: Sasanian Empire
peak: Khosrow I's realm rivaled Byzantium, with a golden age of Persian art, medicine and learning at Gundeshapur.
rise: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians and restored a native Persian dynasty, reviving Zoroastrianism as state religion. The Sasanians fought Rome and Byzantium for 400 years, winning at Edessa and capturing Emperor Valerian.
fall: Exhausted by endless Byzantine wars, the Sasanians were shattered by the Arab Muslim armies in the 630s-40s. The last king, Yazdegerd III, fled east and was murdered near Merv in 651.
legacy: Persian identity, art and administrative tradition that survived into the Islamic era; the word 'shah' and much of Persian court culture.
quizFact: Sasanian silk designs were so admired that Byzantium smuggled silkworms out of China just to compete.

name: Umayyad Caliphate
peak: By 750 it was the largest empire in history to that point, from Spain to the Indus in a single state.
rise: After the first caliphs, the Umayyad family took power and made Islam an imperial force: North Africa, Spain and Central Asia all fell within 90 years. Arabic became the language of government, and Damascus its jewel.
fall: Revolutionaries from the east, backed by those who felt excluded as non-Arab Muslims, destroyed the dynasty in 750. The Abbasids slaughtered the Umayyads at a banquet, though one prince escaped to Spain and founded a rival caliphate in Córdoba.
legacy: Arabic language across three continents, Córdoba's golden culture, and the architectural jewel of the Dome of the Rock.
quizFact: The Umayyads taxed by coin and census, and issued the first Islamic coins with verses from the Quran instead of portraits.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
peak: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad collected and translated the world's knowledge while Europe slept through its early Middle Ages.
rise: The Abbasids rose from a revolution in Khorasan, promising a more inclusive Islamic empire. They founded Baghdad in 762 as a round city of learning, where algebra, astronomy and medicine flourished.
fall: Power slipped to rival dynasties and Turkic guard generals, leaving caliphs as figureheads. In 1258 the Mongol army of Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad so utterly that the Tigris reportedly ran black with ink from thrown books.
legacy: Algebra (al-jabr), preserved Aristotle, hospitals and paper-making, plus 'One Thousand and One Nights' imagery.
quizFact: Baghdad's Round City had four gates facing the four directions, and its founding astrologers picked an auspicious hour to break ground.

name: Ottoman Empire
peak: Suleiman the Magnificent's realm spanned three continents, with the world's finest navy and legal system in the 1500s.
rise: A small Turkish beylik in Anatolia grew under Osman and his heirs: they took Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II, then Serbia, Hungary, Egypt and the Arab lands. Janissaries, devshirme and siege cannons made them the era's superpower.
fall: Slow decline from the late 1600s: failed siege of Vienna in 1683, lost wars with Russia and the Balkan revolts. WWI finished it, the empire was partitioned, and in 1922 Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's new Turkey abolished the sultanate.
legacy: Coffee culture, mosques and bazaars, tulips to Europe, and modern Turkey's borders.
quizFact: Sultans kept giraffes and lions as gifts, and one sultan, Ibrahim I, allegedly had his entire harem thrown into the Bosphorus.
builder: Osman I, a frontier beylik chief in Anatolia around 1299.
reach: Around 5.2 million km2 under Suleiman: Hungary to Yemen, Algeria to the Caucasus, three continents and the entire Mediterranean Arab world.
darkSide: The devshirme system took Christian boys from their families to become janissaries - loyal, but stolen. Succession was fratricide by law: a new sultan's brothers were legally strangled with silk cords, and one sultan killed 19 of them in a single night. The Armenian genocide of 1915, in the empire's dying years, remains its darkest atrocity. Viziers served at the pleasure of the sultan and many lost their heads - literally - when favors turned.
deepLore: The Ottomans ran one of history's most pragmatic machines: Christians and Jews ran as autonomous millets, paid taxes instead of serving, and the Orthodox Patriarch became an Ottoman official. Suleiman's law code shaped the Middle East into modern times. The empire's fatal flaw was succession: fratricide gave way to the Kafes (the Cage), where heirs were imprisoned in the harem until crowned - producing long-reigning fools. By the 1800s the 'Sick Man of Europe' survived only because rivals couldn't agree who got the corpse.

name: Mongol Empire
peak: The largest contiguous land empire ever, ~24 million km², from Korea to Hungary under one Great Khan.
rise: Temüjin united the steppe tribes in 1206 and became Genghis Khan. His horsemen, with composite bows and brutal discipline, crushed Jin China, Khwarezm and the Kievan Rus, moving faster than any army in history.
fall: After Genghis died, the empire split into four khanates among his grandsons. The Yuan dynasty in China was overthrown by Ming rebels in 1368, and the western khanates converted, fragmented and faded.
legacy: The Silk Road's safest era (Pax Mongolica), paper money, the postal relay system (yam), and genetic legacy across Asia.
quizFact: The Mongols created the world's first international postal service, with riders carrying wine pouches as they galloped.
builder: Temujin - Genghis Khan - who united the steppe tribes in 1206.
reach: 24 million km2, the largest contiguous land empire ever: Korea to Hungary, Siberia to Vietnam, conquered mostly within 70 years.
darkSide: Cities that resisted were annihilated as policy: Nishapur's towers were built of skulls, Merv's massacre killed perhaps 700,000, and Baghdad's fall in 1258 drowned the Tigris in books and blood. Merchants who slighted Genghis triggered wars that depopulated whole regions - Khwarezm lost entire cities. Terror was deliberate logistics: word of massacre emptied the next city without a fight. Entire populations were deported as artisan slaves across the steppe.
deepLore: The Mongols ran the world's first globalization: the Yam postal relay moved mail 300 km a day, paper money crossed borders, and the Pax Mongolica let Marco Polo walk from Venice to Khanbaliq. They practiced religious tolerance centuries before Europe, promoted by merit (including women regents), and their law code - the Yassa - banned steppe feuds under pain of death. The empire broke apart because it was held by personality, not institutions: four khanates drifted into local dynasties, and the Black Death traveled their roads home to Europe.

name: Timurid Empire
peak: Timur's realm covered Central Asia, Persia and parts of India, with Samarkand as a wonder of blue-tiled architecture.
rise: Timur (Tamerlane), a Turco-Mongol warlord, claimed Genghis Khan's mantle and conquered from Delhi to Damascus, toppling the Delhi Sultanate, the Mamluks and even crushing the Ottomans at Ankara in 1402.
fall: Timur died in 1405 marching to conquer China. His sons and grandsons fought over the inheritance until the Uzbek Shaybanids took Samarkand in 1507; a Timurid prince, Babur, fled south and founded the Mughal Empire instead.
legacy: Samarkand's Registan, Persian miniatures, gardens and astronomy under Ulugh Beg, and the Mughal dynasty.
quizFact: Timur was lame in one leg from a shepherd youth, but his campaigns killed an estimated 17 million people.

name: Mughal Empire
peak: Under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb it held a quarter of humanity and roughly a quarter of world GDP.
rise: Babur, a Timurid exile, won at Panipat in 1526 with cannon and cavalry, founding a dynasty that fused Persian, Turkic and Indian worlds. Akbar's tolerance and administration built a golden age; Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal.
fall: Aurangzeb's overreach drained the treasury and enraged Hindus and Sikhs. After 1707 Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739, the Marathas and the British East India Company carved away the realms, and the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after the 1857 rebellion.
legacy: The Taj Mahal, Urdu, biryani and Mughlai cuisine, and India's administrative geography.
quizFact: The Peacock Throne was worth more than the rest of the empire's yearly income, covered in rubies and emeralds.
builder: Babur, a Timurid prince exiled from Samarkand, who won Panipat with cannon in 1526.
reach: Around 4 million km2 under Aurangzeb - nearly the whole subcontinent, a quarter of humanity and perhaps 25% of world GDP.
darkSide: Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya tax on Hindus, demolished temples and warred for 26 years in the Deccan, bleeding the treasury white. Succession was open war: Shah Jahan's sons fought so brutally that Aurangzeb executed two brothers and imprisoned his own father for his last eight years above the Taj Mahal. War elephants and scorched-earth campaigns depopulated whole provinces; Rajput and Sikh uprisings were answered with massacres.
deepLore: The Mughals fused three worlds - Persian court culture, Turkic cavalry tradition, and India's own genius - into an empire of the Taj Mahal, Urdu poetry, miniature painting and Mughlai cuisine. Akbar married Rajput princesses, abolished the jizya and ran a faith-agnostic court; his revenue system (the zabti) was so fair it survived the empire. The rot began with Aurangzeb's orthodoxy: Marathas, Sikhs and the British East India Company each ate a slice until 1857, when the last Mughal - a poet-king - was exiled to Rangoon and his sons shot by a British captain.

name: Maurya Empire
peak: Under Ashoka it ruled nearly the whole subcontinent, one of the largest empires of its age.
rise: Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the strategist Chanakya, toppled the Nanda dynasty and seized the Ganges plain, then beat back Seleucus Nicator's Greeks. His grandson Ashoka conquered Kalinga, then renounced war after seeing its horror.
fall: Ashoka's pacifism drained the treasury of military vigor; successors lost provinces, and the last Mauryan king was assassinated by his Brahmin general Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BC.
legacy: Buddhism's spread across Asia, Ashoka's rock edicts (India's first writing), and India's national emblem, the Lion Capital.
quizFact: Ashoka's edicts are so widespread that they form India's earliest readable inscriptions, some carved beside highways still in use.

name: Gupta Empire
peak: The classical golden age of India: zero, decimal math, Kalidasa's poetry and Nalanda University.
rise: Sri Gupta's line rose to power under Chandragupta I and Samudragupta, whose conquests across the Ganges plain set up 200 years of peace and prosperity. Science, art and Sanskrit literature blossomed at court.
fall: Hun invasions (the Hephthalites) and rising vassals broke the empire apart by 550. India splintered into regional kingdoms for centuries.
legacy: The concept of zero, decimal system, Aryabhata's astronomy, and classical Hindu temple art.
quizFact: Aryabhata calculated the Earth's rotation and the length of the year to within minutes, using no telescope.

name: British Empire
peak: By 1920 it covered about a quarter of the world's land and people, the largest empire in history.
rise: Piracy, trade and colonization: from Virginia and the Caribbean to the East India Company's conquest of Bengal after Plassey (1757). The Industrial Revolution and the Royal Navy gave Britain the muscle to rule waves, taking India, Africa and Oceania.
fall: Two world wars drained the treasury and the colonies' loyalty. India left in 1947, the Suez fiasco of 1956 showed the decline, and Hong Kong's handover in 1997 closed the book.
legacy: English as the world language, cricket and tea culture, parliaments and railways across continents, and borders still disputed today.
quizFact: At its height, the sun literally never set on the empire: there was always daylight on at least one territory.
builder: Merchant companies and crown charters - the East India Company, the Virginia Company - before Parliament took over.
reach: 35.5 million km2, a quarter of the world's land and people: India, Canada, Australia, half of Africa, islands on every ocean.
darkSide: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed around 3 million under Churchill's war cabinet while grain ships passed by; the Amritsar massacre of 1919 shot 1,000 unarmed Indians in ten minutes. The Atlantic slave trade ran on British ships for 150 years. Australia's settler frontier devastated Aboriginal nations; concentration camps were pioneered in the Boer War, where 26,000 women and children died. Ireland lost a million to famine under export-protecting landlordism.
deepLore: Britain's trick was ruling on the cheap: one civil servant per 200,000 Indians, governing through princes, landlords and sepoys. It built 100,000 km of Indian railways - mostly to move cotton and troops. The empire's endgame was seeded by its own education: Gandhi, Nehru and Kenyatta learned law and self-determination in London. In 1947 the Raj was partitioned in six weeks; a million died in the Partition massacres, the empire's last and largest wound.

name: Spanish Empire
peak: The first empire on which 'the sun never set', from Mexico and Peru to the Philippines.
rise: Columbus sailed for Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492; within a century Cortés toppled the Aztecs and Pizarro the Incas, and silver from Potosí made Spain Europe's superpower with the Armada as its shield.
fall: Silver inflation, endless European wars and the Armada's 1588 defeat started the slide. Napoleon's 1808 invasion triggered independence revolutions by Bolívar and San Martín, and the 1898 war with the US took Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines.
legacy: Spanish across the Americas, Catholicism, hacienda culture, and the world's second-most spoken language.
quizFact: Potosí's mountain in Bolivia yielded so much silver that 'worth a Potosí' became a Spanish expression for riches.
builder: The Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, who funded Columbus and finished the Reconquista in 1492.
reach: About 13.7 million km2 - the Americas from California to Tierra del Fuego, the Philippines, the Low Countries and parts of Italy.
darkSide: The conquistadors butchered their way across two continents: Tenochtitlan's siege killed 100,000+ in 1521, Pizarro strangled the Inca state after executing Atahualpa over a roomful of ransom gold. The encomienda system worked indigenous populations to death in mines like Potosi, where millions died; smallpox and measles erased perhaps 90% of the Americas' people within a century - the greatest demographic collapse in human history. The Inquisition burned heretics at home and abroad.
deepLore: Spain's empire was run from a desk in Seville - the Casa de Contratacion licensed every ship, every migrant, every map (its master chart was a state secret). Silver from Potosi and Mexico funded Habsburg wars across Europe and inflated the world economy for a century, then vanished into Dutch and English banks when Spanish debt crashed. The empire's enlightenment came too late: reformers like Charles III modernized too slowly, and when Napoleon kidnapped the Spanish king in 1808, America's colonies declared home rule and never looked back.

name: Portuguese Empire
peak: A trading empire from Brazil to Macau, the first global sea power, armed with the caravel and the astrolabe.
rise: Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored voyages down Africa's coast; Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Portugal seized Goa, Malacca and Hormuz, dominating the spice trade with forts from Africa to Asia.
fall: Too small to police the world, Portugal lost trade to the Dutch and English in the 1600s. Brazil left peacefully in 1822, Africa's colonies in the 1970s after a long war, and Macau returned to China in 1999.
legacy: Portuguese in Brazil, Angola, Mozambique and Goa; the world's map sketching of Africa and Asia; caipirinha's spirit, cachaça.
quizFact: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas literally divided the non-European world between Portugal and Spain with a line on a map.

name: French Empire (Napoleonic)
peak: In 1812 Napoleon ruled or allied with most of continental Europe from Madrid to Moscow.
rise: A Corsican artillery officer rode the French Revolution's chaos to power, crowned himself Emperor in 1804, and rewrote European war: Austerlitz, Jena, and the Code Napoleon, whose civil law still shapes half the world.
fall: The 1812 invasion of Russia swallowed Moscow but not the winter; half a million men froze or starved. Refusing a fair peace, Napoleon lost at Leipzig, abdicated, returned for the Hundred Days, and fell for good at Waterloo in 1815.
legacy: The Napoleonic Code, metric system, meritocracy in government, and the shape of modern Europe.
quizFact: Napoleon's soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, which let scholars finally read Egyptian hieroglyphs.
builder: Napoleon Bonaparte, a minor Corsican artillery noble who seized a revolution.
reach: Around 2.1 million km2 directly, with vassals and allies ruling from Barcelona to Warsaw - 44 million subjects at the 1812 peak.
darkSide: The Napoleonic Wars killed 3.5-6 million people across Europe. Spain's Peninsular War saw guerrillas and French reprisals commit mutual atrocities that torched whole provinces. Napoleon restored slavery in the colonies in 1802, triggering a Haitian war of extermination; his failed Russian invasion left perhaps 400,000 of his own men frozen or starved. He crowned himself emperor of a republic he had already strangled.
deepLore: Napoleon's true weapon was not the bayonet but the Code - civil law by merit, not birth, exported to every land his armies crossed and still the backbone of law on four continents. He centralized science (Egyptology was born from his expedition), standardized weights, and sold Louisiana to fund his wars. His genius and his hubris were the same instinct: Austerlitz was won by giving away ground; Moscow was lost the same way. Exiled to Elba, he returned for the Hundred Days - and Waterloo ended 20 years of continental war in one rainy afternoon.

name: Dutch Colonial Empire
peak: The VOC (Dutch East India Company) was the richest company in history, worth more than Apple and Google combined today.
rise: Independence from Spain freed the Dutch to sail: they invented modern capitalism (first stock market, 1602), seized Malacca and Ceylon, founded Cape Town and New Amsterdam (which became New York), and ran the spice trade from Batavia.
fall: Britain out-traded the Dutch and took New Amsterdam in 1664; Java's wars and nationalism ended the East Indies, which became Indonesia in 1949 after a brutal independence struggle.
legacy: Dutch place names from Harlem to Bushwick, tulips to New York, Indonesian food in the Netherlands, and the world's first multinational.
quizFact: The VOC paid its investors an average 18% annual return for nearly 200 years, the most successful company ever.

name: Holy Roman Empire
peak: A thousand-year patchwork of 1,800 states, duchies, bishoprics and free cities under an elected emperor.
rise: Charlemagne's coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800 revived a western 'Roman' crown. The empire fused German, Italian and Burgundian lands with the Church, emperors and popes crowning and fighting each other for a millennium.
fall: Voltaire's quip held true: neither holy, Roman, nor an empire. Napoleon crushed it at Austerlitz, and in 1806 Emperor Francis II simply dissolved the ancient title, becoming Emperor of Austria instead.
legacy: Germany's federal tradition, cathedral cities and castles, the Habsburg legacy, and the medieval idea of Christendom.
quizFact: The emperor was elected by seven (later nine) prince-electors, which is why the German emperor was never simply inherited at first.

name: Habsburg (Austro-Hungarian) Empire
peak: Charles V ruled Spain, the Americas, Austria, the Netherlands and half of Italy, an empire where 'the sun never set' too.
rise: The Habsburgs won by marriage: 'Bella gerant alii, tu felix Austria nube' (let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry). From Vienna they ruled the Holy Roman Empire, then built the dual Austro-Hungarian monarchy in 1867 with waltzes, coffeehouses and 11 nationalities.
fall: Nationalism and the Balkans pulled the empire apart. The 1914 assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo ignited WWI; four years of defeat ended with the empire dissolving overnight into Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.
legacy: Vienna's music (Mozart to Strauss), kaffeehaus culture, a multilingual bureaucracy, and the powder keg of WWI.
quizFact: Empress Maria Theresa had 16 children and married them into every royal house of Europe, earning the nickname 'the grandmother of Europe'.

name: German Empire (Prussia-led)
peak: Europe's industrial and military powerhouse, with the world's best universities and chemical industry.
rise: Otto von Bismarck engineered unification by 'blood and iron': wars with Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1871) forged 25 German states into an empire, proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, an insult France never forgot.
fall: Bismarck's successors fumbled diplomacy into WWI. Four years of trench warfare ended with collapse at home; Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated in November 1918, and the Treaty of Versailles dismembered the empire.
legacy: Germany's industrial might, autobahns' ancestor, social insurance (Bismarck invented pensions), and the road to two world wars.
quizFact: Bismarck predicted 'some damned foolish thing in the Balkans' would ignite the next great war, 20 years before Sarajevo.

name: Russian Empire
peak: One-sixth of Earth's land, from Poland to Alaska (until 1867) under the Tsars.
rise: Peter the Great dragged Russia to the Baltic, built St Petersburg and modernized the army; Catherine the Great added Crimea and Poland's shares. By 1890 the empire was Europe's largest population and a colossus of land and serfs.
fall: WWI broke the empire: food riots, mutinies and the February Revolution of 1917 forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate. The Bolsheviks executed the family in 1918, and the world's first communist state rose from the rubble.
legacy: Russian literature (Tolstoy, Dostoevsky), the Trans-Siberian railway, and the vast multi-ethnic map that became the USSR.
quizFact: Russia sold Alaska to the US in 1867 for $7.2 million, about two cents per acre.
builder: Peter the Great, who westernized the state and beat Sweden at Poltava; Catherine the Great expanded it.
reach: 22.8 million km2 by 1866, from Poland to Alaska across eleven time zones, 125 million people by 1897.
darkSide: Serfdom bound the majority until 1861 - decades after the rest of Europe abolished it - and land hunger kept them poor. The Pale of Settlement confined Jews to the west; pogroms were tolerated and sometimes organized. Poland was partitioned out of existence and its 1830 and 1863 uprisings crushed with deportations to Siberia. The Okhrana secret police and the katorga penal system became synonyms of tyranny.
deepLore: Russia's empire was a paradox: a European great power that exported grain worldwide, yet a state where 80% of people could not read their tsar's name. It produced Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky and Mendeleev while famine stalked the villages. The Trans-Siberian railway stitched the giant together in 1904 - too late for the war with Japan. WWI broke the state in weeks: bread queues became revolution, and the Romanov 300-year dynasty ended in a cellar in Yekaterinburg.

name: Soviet Union
peak: Post-1945 superpower, first in space with Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961), rival of the USA.
rise: From the 1917 revolution, Lenin and then Stalin built a one-party state of collectivized farms and crash industrialization. The USSR absorbed the blow of Hitler's invasion, took Berlin in 1945, and emerged as one of two superpowers.
fall: Economic stagnation, the Afghanistan quagmire and Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost, perestroika) opened the floodgates. In December 1991 the union dissolved into 15 countries, ending the Cold War almost without a fight.
legacy: Spaceflight's firsts, the KGB's legend, Russian as the lingua franca of half the planet, and the nuclear arsenal it left behind.
quizFact: The USSR's last president, Gorbachev, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990, a year before his own state vanished.
builder: Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks, who seized the collapsing Russian state in October 1917.
reach: 22.4 million km2, one-sixth of the planet, with influence across Eastern Europe, Cuba, Vietnam and half of Africa's revolutions.
darkSide: Stalin's rule killed millions: the Holodomor famine in Ukraine (1932-33) took about 3.5 million, the Great Purge shot 700,000 in two years, and the Gulag archipelago worked 18 million prisoners at any time. The 1939 partition of Poland with Hitler included the Katyn massacre of 22,000 Polish officers. Hungary 1956 and Prague 1968 were crushed by tanks; Afghanistan became its Vietnam.
deepLore: The USSR was history's fastest industrial revolution - from wooden plows to Sputnik in 40 years, at a human cost no democracy could have imposed. It beat the Nazis at Stalingrad and took Berlin, losing 27 million people. Its science schools (mathematics, space, nuclear) remain world-class. But central planning couldn't price a screw: by the 1980s queues, not missiles, defeated it. Gorbachev tried to reform a one-party state into an open one and discovered the contradiction - openness dissolved it in 1,236 days.

name: Qing Dynasty
peak: Under Qianlong, the largest economy on Earth and a realm of 13 million km² from Tibet to Taiwan.
rise: The Manchus swept through the Great Wall in 1644 when Ming allies opened the gates at Shanhaiguan. Kangxi and Qianlong expanded China to its greatest extent, and the empire's population exploded past 400 million.
fall: The Opium Wars (1839-42, 1856-60) forced treaties, ports and Hong Kong onto the British. The Taiping Rebellion killed 20 million, and after the 1911 Xinhai Revolution the last emperor, Puyi, abdicated at age six.
legacy: China's modern borders, the Forbidden City's grandeur, Peking opera and cuisine, and the 'century of humiliation' that still shapes Chinese politics.
quizFact: The Qing 'Queue Order' forced every Han Chinese man to shave his forehead and braid the rest, on pain of death.
builder: Nurhaci and his son Hong Taiji, who unified the Manchu tribes; the Ming let them through the Wall in 1644.
reach: 13.1 million km2 at its height - Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia, Taiwan - China largest-ever territory and 450 million people by 1900.
darkSide: The conquest massacres of Yangzhou and Jiading set the tone; the Queue Order made haircutting a capital issue. The Dzungar genocide (1755-57) wiped out an entire Mongol people. Later, the Taiping Rebellion (triggered by Qing misrule) killed 20-30 million, and Empress Dowager Cixi diverted navy funds to rebuild a marble boat while the empire drowned.
deepLore: The Qing was China most successful dynasty and its most humiliating - both true. Its emperors (Kangxi, Qianlong) ran a multi-ethnic empire with a Manchu core, Confucian administration and steppe diplomacy, doubling the state size. But it met industrial Europe with a tribute worldview: the Opium Wars, unequal treaties and Hong Kong loss began the Century of Humiliation that still drives Chinese politics. In 1912 a six-year-old emperor abdicated; two millennia of imperial China ended with a regent signature.

name: Ming Dynasty
peak: The Forbidden City built, the Great Wall in brick, and Zheng He's treasure fleets sailing to Africa.
rise: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant monk turned warlord, expelled the Mongols and founded the Ming in 1368. The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, built the Forbidden City, and sent Zheng He's giant treasure ships to India, Arabia and East Africa.
fall: Isolationism, silver inflation and the Little Ice Age's famines hollowed the state. In 1644 rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing; the last Ming emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill, and the Manchus marched through the opened gates.
legacy: The Great Wall we know today, the Forbidden City, blue-and-white porcelain, and the novel as a Chinese art form.
quizFact: Zheng He's treasure ships were possibly 120 m long, four times the size of Columbus's flagship, sailing 90 years before him.

name: Han Dynasty
peak: Contemporaneous with Rome at its height, ~60 million people, the Silk Road's western march.
rise: Liu Bang, a peasant-born rebel, won the civil wars after Qin's collapse and founded the Han. The dynasty adopted Confucian bureaucracy, opened the Silk Road under Zhang Qian, and invented paper in 105 AD.
fall: Court eunuchs, child emperors and the Yellow Turban Rebellion tore the state apart. In 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, and China split into the Three Kingdoms, an era later immortalized in epic romance.
legacy: China's majority 'Han' ethnic identity, Confucian state exams, paper, and the Silk Road to Rome.
quizFact: Han emperors were buried in jade suits sewn with gold wire, thousands of jade plates each, to preserve the body forever.

name: Empire of Japan
peak: The dominant power of Asia by 1942, with an empire from Korea to New Guinea.
rise: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 industrialized Japan at breakneck speed; it beat China (1895) and Russia (1905), annexed Korea (1910), and seized Manchuria and coastal China in the 1930s under militarist rule.
fall: Pearl Harbor (1941) brought the US into WWII; by 1945 firebombing and two atomic bombs forced surrender. American occupation rewrote Japan as a peaceful democracy; Emperor Hirohito renounced divine status.
legacy: Post-war Japan's industrial miracle, anime and tech, the atomic age's memory, and East Asia's modern borders.
quizFact: Japan's 1905 victory over Russia was the first modern defeat of a European power by an Asian nation, shocking the world.
builder: The Meiji oligarchs - samurai who toppled the shogun in 1868 and industrialized at forced speed.
reach: About 7.4 million km2 at its 1942 height: Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria, coastal China, Southeast Asia and the Pacific islands.
darkSide: The 1937 Nanjing massacre killed 200,000-300,000 Chinese civilians in six weeks; Unit 731 ran biological warfare experiments on living prisoners. The 'comfort women' system enslaved up to 200,000 women across Asia. Korean and Taiwanese subjects were forced into labor and language; the Three Alls policy in China - kill all, burn all, loot all - devastated the north. The end came only after two atomic bombs.
deepLore: Japan did in 40 years what Europe took 400 to do: feudal island to carrier navy. Victory over Russia in 1905 electrified colonized Asia - here was proof Europe could be beaten. The empire's tragedy was structural: the army answered only to the emperor, and young officers assassinated moderating ministers until the state could not stop its own generals. After 1945 the same industriousness rebuilt Japan into an economic superpower under a constitution that renounced war - written in six days by American lawyers.

name: Khmer Empire
peak: Angkor was the world's largest pre-industrial city, possibly 1,000 temples and 750,000 people.
rise: Jayavarman II declared himself 'universal ruler' in 802, founding a dynasty of god-kings (devarajas). Successors built reservoirs, canals and temples across Cambodia, culminating in Suryavarman II's Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth.
fall: Drought, war with Siam (Ayutthaya) and the sacking of Angkor in 1431 ended the capital. The court moved to Phnom Penh, and the jungle swallowed the temples for centuries.
legacy: Angkor Wat on Cambodia's flag, the greatest archaeological site in Southeast Asia, and Khmer art and dance.
quizFact: Angkor's hydraulic engineers built a reservoir 8 km by 2 km, the West Baray, big enough to be seen from space.

name: Srivijaya Empire
peak: Master of the Strait of Malacca, the choke point of all East-West trade for 600 years.
rise: A Buddhist thalassocracy: Srivijaya grew rich taxing every ship between India and China, and made Palembang a center of Buddhist learning that drew Chinese pilgrims like Yijing to study Sanskrit.
fall: Indian Chola raiders devastated the realm in 1025, and rising Javanese and Malay ports drained its trade. By 1288 it vanished into the Majapahit orbit, remembered only in Chinese records until modern archaeology.
legacy: The spread of Buddhism through Maritime Southeast Asia, Malay as a trade lingua franca, and Indonesia's maritime identity.
quizFact: For centuries scholars only knew Srivijaya from Chinese and Indian texts until French archaeologist George Coedès rediscovered it in 1918.

name: Mali Empire
peak: The richest man in history was Mali's Mansa Musa, whose 1324 gold pilgrimage crashed Cairo's economy.
rise: Sundiata Keita, the 'Lion King' of the Mande epic, crushed the Sosso at Kirina (1235) and forged a federation of 12 kingdoms. Mali's gold mines and control of trans-Saharan trade made Timbuktu a legend of wealth and learning.
fall: Mansa Musa's heirs fought civil wars; the Songhai rose in the east, and Moroccan invasions with firearms (1591) shattered the realm. Mali shrank to a rump state and faded by the 1670s.
legacy: Timbuktu's Sankore University and manuscripts, the image of African gold, and griot storytelling traditions.
quizFact: Mansa Musa handed out so much gold in Cairo that its value collapsed for 12 years, the only recorded case of a person crashing a currency.

name: Songhai Empire
peak: The largest empire in West African history, bigger than Mali, from Senegal to Niger.
rise: Sunni Ali built the empire with river fleets and cavalry, taking Timbuktu and Djenné; his successor Askia Muhammad organized it with ministries, tax courts and Islamic scholarship, making Timbuktu's libraries rival Cairo's.
fall: Askia's sons fought over the throne, and in 1591 a small Moroccan army with muskets and cannons crossed the Sahara and destroyed the Songhai at Tondibi, a classic case of gunpowder beating numbers.
legacy: Timbuktu's manuscript libraries, the Niger river cities, and West Africa's scholarly golden age.
quizFact: Timbuktu's librarians still preserve hundreds of thousands of ancient manuscripts, some hidden in family trunks for centuries.

name: Aksumite Empire
peak: A Red Sea trade colossus listed by the Persian prophet Mani among the four great powers of the age.
rise: Aksum grew rich exporting ivory, gold and frankincense between Africa, Rome and India. King Ezana converted to Christianity around 330, making it one of the first Christian states, and minted coins with the cross.
fall: Rising Islamic powers shifted Red Sea trade away; climate stress and the Beja migrations chipped at the core. Aksum faded by the 10th century, its legacy passing to the Zagwe and Solomonic dynasties.
legacy: Ethiopia's Orthodox Christianity, the Ge'ez script, giant stelae, and the legend of the Ark of the Covenant at Aksum.
quizFact: Aksum's tallest obelisk stood 33 m and weighed 520 tonnes, carved from a single piece of granite.

name: Kingdom of Kush
peak: The 25th Dynasty: Kushite pharaohs actually ruled all of Egypt for a century.
rise: Rising on the Nile south of Egypt, Kush mastered iron and gold. King Piye conquered Egypt in 727 BC and founded the 25th Dynasty of 'Black Pharaohs', building pyramids by the dozen at Napata and Meroë.
fall: Assyrian armies with iron weapons pushed the Kushites out of Egypt by 656 BC. The kingdom retreated south to Meroë, thrived for another 900 years, then declined as trade routes shifted and Aksum rose; it fell around 550 AD.
legacy: More pyramids than Egypt (Sudan has ~250), Meroitic script still partly unread, and the legend of Candace, the warrior queen.
quizFact: Kushite queens called Kandake led armies; one, Amanirenas, fought Rome to a standstill with one eye lost in battle.

name: Carthaginian Empire
peak: Master of the western Mediterranean, with trade colonies from Spain to Sicily and silver from Iberia.
rise: Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded Carthage in 814 BC; it outgrew its mother city with trade, silver from Spain, and a navy of quinqueremes. Hannibal's elephants crossed the Alps in 218 BC and shocked Rome for 15 years.
fall: Rome feared Carthage to the end: after the Punic Wars, Cato demanded 'Carthago delenda est' (Carthage must be destroyed). Scipio Aemilianus razed the city in 146 BC, selling survivors into slavery, though Rome later rebuilt it.
legacy: The alphabet we use came via Phoenician; Mediterranean trade law, and Hannibal's legend as history's great tactician.
quizFact: Hannibal lost an eye crossing the Alps but never lost a major battle in Italy, yet still lost the war.

name: New Kingdom of Egypt
peak: Egypt's golden empire from the Euphrates to Sudan, with Tutankhamun, Ramesses II and the Valley of the Kings.
rise: Ahmose I drove out the Hyksos and launched Egypt's imperial age. Thutmose III marched to the Euphrates, Ramesses II dueled the Hittites at Kadesh and signed history's first recorded peace treaty, and pharaohs buried themselves in golden splendor.
fall: Sea Peoples raided the coasts around 1177 BC, Nubia broke away, and priest-kings of Amun swallowed the throne. Egypt fragmented into the Third Intermediate Period, its imperial age over.
legacy: The pyramids' successors: tombs like Tutankhamun's, Karnak and Abu Simbel, and Egyptology itself.
quizFact: Tutankhamun's tomb was found in 1922 with 5,398 objects, including 143 gold pieces, after 3,000 years undisturbed.

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
peak: The world's first true empire, with the largest army, library and city of its time.
rise: Iron weapons, siege engines and terror tactics built Assyria's dominance from Babylon to Egypt. Kings Ashurnasirpal, Tiglath-Pileser III and Ashurbanipal deported populations, built roads, and collected the world's first great library.
fall: Enemies circled when Ashurbanipal died: Babylonians, Medes and Scythians combined, and in 612 BC a coalition burned Nineveh so completely that Greek travelers later forgot where it lay. The empire vanished within 20 years.
legacy: The library's clay tablets (including the Epic of Gilgamesh), Assyrian reliefs, and the ruthless imperial model others copied.
quizFact: Ashurbanipal's library held 30,000 tablets, and its Epic of Gilgamesh includes a flood story older than Noah's.

name: Aztec (Triple Alliance) Empire
peak: A lake capital of 200,000 people with floating gardens, larger than most European cities of the time.
rise: The Mexica, once desert nomads, built Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco and allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan in 1428. Tribute, chinampa farming and warrior cults made the Triple Alliance the masters of Mesoamerica.
fall: Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519 with 600 men, cannons, horses, smallpox and thousands of native allies. After the Noche Triste retreat, his siege and disease took Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Emperor Cuauhtémoc was captured on Lake Texcoco.
legacy: Mexico City on the old lakebed, Nahuatl words like chocolate and tomato, and the Mexica sun stone calendar.
quizFact: Tenochtitlan's aqueducts and street lighting amazed Spanish conquistadors, who said they were 'walking in a dream'.

name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)
peak: The largest empire in pre-Columbian America, 12 million people and 40,000 km of stone roads.
rise: Pachacuti ('earth-shaker') rebuilt Cusco and conquered the Andes from 1438, linking Ecuador to Chile with roads, terraces, quipu record-keeping and storehouses. Machu Picchu was his royal estate.
fall: Civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar weakened the empire just as Francisco Pizarro landed in 1532. The Spanish captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca, took a roomful of gold ransom and killed him anyway; resistance lingered until 1572.
legacy: Quechua still spoken by millions, Machu Picchu, potato and quinoa agriculture, and Inca stonework that shrugs off earthquakes.
quizFact: The Incas kept records with knotted strings (quipu) instead of writing, and some knots still defy decoding.

name: Zulu Kingdom
peak: Shaka's impi regiments ruled 250,000 km² of southern Africa, defeating a British army at Isandlwana (1879).
rise: Shaka Zulu revolutionized warfare with the short stabbing spear, 'buffalo horns' tactics and age-regiments, forging a nation from clans. His successors Cetshwayo and Dingane kept the kingdom the strongest in southern Africa.
fall: The British wanted Natal secure: after Isandlwana's shock defeat (1,300 redcoats died), they returned with overwhelming force and guns, taking Ulundi in 1879. The kingdom was broken into fragments and absorbed by 1897.
legacy: Zulu language and pride, the legend of Shaka, and South Africa's cultural tapestry.
quizFact: At Isandlwana 20,000 Zulu warriors wiped out a British column armed with rifles and artillery, one of the worst defeats a colonial army ever suffered.

name: Babylonian Empire
peak: Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon was the largest city on Earth, ringed by walls so thick a chariot could turn on top, home to the Ishtar Gate and the legendary Hanging Gardens.
rise: Hammurabi turned a river town into an empire around 1750 BC with the world's first written law code - 282 rules carved on a black stone pillar. Centuries later Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt it into the wonder of the ancient world, conquering Jerusalem in 587 BC and marching its elite to exile in Babylon.
fall: In 539 BC Cyrus the Great took Babylon in one night by diverting the Euphrates and walking his army under the walls - as the regent Belshazzar feasted, per the Book of Daniel. Babylon kept blooming under Persians and Greeks until its bricks were carted off to build other cities.
legacy: The 60-minute hour, 360-degree circle, base-60 math, written law, and the epic of Gilgamesh all come from Babylon's scribes.
quizFact: Hammurabi's Code included consumer protection: a builder whose house collapsed and killed the owner was himself put to death.
builder: Hammurabi the lawgiver; Nebuchadnezzar II the builder-king.
reach: Mesopotamia and the Levant - roughly 100,000 km2 - small in land but the intellectual superpower of the ancient Near East for 1,300 years.
darkSide: Jerusalem's two sieges ended with the city burned, the Temple razed and Judah's elite marched to captivity in 587 BC - the Babylonian Exile. Rebellious cities were deported wholesale, their populations swapped like livestock to break identity.

name: Hittite Empire
peak: The first empire of iron, fielding the chariot armies that fought Egypt's Ramesses II to a standstill at Kadesh (1274 BC) - history's earliest recorded great battle.
rise: An Indo-European people in Anatolia who mastered iron smelting and chariot warfare, the Hittites sacked Babylon in 1595 BC and built a state of fortified rock cities. Their legal code fined crimes instead of maiming - startlingly humane for the Bronze Age.
fall: The Bronze Age Collapse (around 1180 BC) - drought, famine, the Sea Peoples and internal collapse - burned Hattusa and erased the empire within a generation. Scribes stopped writing; the capital lay forgotten for 3,000 years until excavated in 1906.
legacy: Iron working spread to the world from their forges; the Treaty of Kadesh with Egypt is the oldest surviving peace treaty - its copy hangs at the UN.
quizFact: The Hittites signed the world's first peace treaty - with Egypt - 3,200 years before the United Nations printed a copy.
builder: Kings like Suppiluliuma I and Muwatalli II of the Hattusa dynasty.
reach: Anatolia and northern Syria, about 300,000 km2 - the superpower that checked Egypt and toppled Babylon.
darkSide: Hittite raids deported whole populations to work royal estates, and their succession was a century of fratricide - queen mothers poisoned princes and princes murdered brothers. Sack of Babylon aside, their vassal treaties promised enslavement for rebellion in clause after clause.

name: Delhi Sultanate
peak: Five dynasties deep, it ruled nearly the whole subcontinent north of the Deccan and built Delhi into one of the world's largest cities.
rise: Born from the leftovers of Muhammad Ghori's conquest, the slave-general Qutb al-Din Aibak founded a Turkic dynasty in Delhi in 1206. Under Alauddin Khalji the sultanate repelled the Mongols repeatedly, fixed prices by decree and raided the fabled southern kingdoms.
fall: 1526: Babur's cannons and cavalry destroyed the last Lodi sultan at Panipat - the same battle that founded the Mughal Empire on the sultanate's bones.
legacy: The Qutb Minar, Indo-Islamic architecture, Urdu's birth from camp languages, and Delhi's rise as India's political center.
quizFact: Alauddin Khalji's market reforms fixed prices so strictly that a broken weight was punished by cutting an equal piece of flesh from the shopkeeper.
builder: Qutb al-Din Aibak, a Turkic slave who rose to kingship - the Mamluk (slave) dynasty.
reach: Most of the Indian subcontinent at its height, around 2.5 million km2 under Alauddin Khalji.
darkSide: Khalji's Gujarat and Devagiri campaigns enslaved tens of thousands; Mongol prisoners were trampled by elephants. Temple taxation (jizya) and the sack of brilliant cities like Devagiri marked the conquest; Timur's 1398 sack of Delhi - killing 100,000 of its own citizens in a day - came when the sultanate was too weak to stop it.

name: Vijayanagara Empire
peak: Krishnadevaraya's Hampi: a city of 500,000 - larger than any in Europe at the time - of gold-leafed temples, aqueducts and one of the world's great bazaars.
rise: Founded in 1336 by brothers Harihara and Bukka to defend Hindu kingdoms against the Delhi Sultanate's southern raids, Vijayanagara ('City of Victory') grew into a 300-year shield and a golden age of Telugu and Kannada literature.
fall: The Battle of Talikota (1565): five allied sultanates destroyed the army and sacked Hampi for six months. The city was never rebuilt - its stone chariots and temples still stand in ruins, a UNESCO site.
legacy: Hampi's ruins, Carnatic music's patronage, and the survival of southern Hindu political power for two more centuries.
quizFact: Foreign traders wrote that in Hampi's markets diamonds were sold by the heap, not the stone - people simply poured them out like grain.
builder: Brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty.
reach: All of South India and parts of the Deccan, about 500,000 km2 under Krishnadevaraya.
darkSide: Krishnadevaraya's wars against the Bahmani sultanates featured mass executions of captured garrisons; the empire's own succession was rotten - royal sons poisoned fathers and the 1565 defeat ended in the sacking and massacre of Hampi's civilians.

name: Ayutthaya Kingdom (Siam)
peak: One of the world's great trading ports: by 1700 Ayutthaya had a million residents - more than London - with Japanese, Persian, Portuguese and Chinese quarters on its canals.
rise: Founded by U Thong in 1351 on the Chao Phraya floodplain, Ayutthaya fused Khmer administration with Thai power, dominating the Malay peninsula and the China trade for 400 years.
fall: In 1767 the Burmese army sacked the city after a 14-month siege, burning the temples and beheading the Buddha images. The court fled south and founded Bangkok - the Chakri dynasty that still reigns.
legacy: Modern Thailand's royal institution, Ayutthaya's ruined temples (a UNESCO site), and the only Southeast Asian state never colonized by Europe.
quizFact: Ayutthaya's king kept a Japanese samurai bodyguard corps, and one of them - Yamada Nagamasa - became a provincial governor.
builder: King U Thong (Ramathibodi I), a refugee prince who married into Lopburi royalty.
reach: The Chao Phraya basin and the Malay peninsula - tribute from Laos, Cambodia and the Shan states.
darkSide: Court politics were lethal: usurpations killed six dynasties of kings, and succession struggles between princes were settled by elephant duels to the death. Wars with Burma and the Khmer included mass deportations of entire cities' populations to Siam's rice fields.

name: Asante Empire
peak: The gold coast's superpower: a disciplined army of 200,000, a capital of British-comparable street lighting, and the Golden Stool as the living soul of the nation.
rise: Osei Tutu and the priest Okomfo Anokye united the Asante clans around the Golden Stool (1701) and built a federation of tribute states that out-organized every rival on the Guinea coast, controlling the gold and kola trade with Europeans.
fall: Four Anglo-Asante wars; in 1900, when a British governor demanded to sit on the Golden Stool, the Asante went to war one last time under Yaa Asantewaa - a queen mother in her 60s. Britain annexed the empire in 1902.
legacy: Ghana's modern identity, kente cloth, Adinkra symbols, and the Golden Stool - never surrendered, still enthroned in Kumasi.
quizFact: The Golden Stool was never sat on - not even by kings - and when the British demanded it in 1900, the Asante went to war rather than hand it over.
builder: Osei Tutu with the priest Okomfo Anokye, who 'conjured' the Golden Stool from the sky.
reach: About 250,000 km2 of West Africa's gold forests, from the Volta to the Ivory Coast.
darkSide: Asante's power ran on tribute and terror: rebellious vassals were sacrificed in mass ceremonies (human sacrifice at royal funerals reached the hundreds), and the state raided neighbors for captives to work gold fields and trade with coastal slavers.

name: Kingdom of Benin
peak: Benin City in 1691: walls four times longer than the Great Wall of China in combined length, streets lit at night by palm-oil lamps - Europe's envoys called it 'Great Benin'.
rise: The Edo kingdom grew from the 12th century into West Africa's artistic superpower, its brass plaques and heads (cast by the guild of bronze-smiths since the 1200s) documenting 700 years of kings and conquests.
fall: The 1897 British punitive expedition: troops burned the city and looted thousands of brasses and ivories, which now sit in museums across Europe and America. The Oba was exiled; the monarchy survives today as a traditional throne.
legacy: The Benin Bronzes - among the greatest artworks ever made in Africa - and the current global debate over returning looted heritage.
quizFact: Benin City's earthworks stretched 16,000 km - four times the length of the Great Wall of China - enclosing a city that impressed Portuguese visitors more than Lisbon.
builder: The Oba dynasty, said to descend from Ife's Oduduwa lineage - consolidated by Oba Ewuare the Great in the 1400s.
reach: The Edo forest belt between the Niger and Lagos, trading pepper, cloth and ivory to Portugal and the Netherlands.
darkSide: Benin was a slave-trading partner of the Atlantic trade for two centuries, and its court ritually sacrificed servants at royal funerals. Its prosperity rested on the same human commerce that emptied the African coast.

name: Kievan Rus
peak: Under Yaroslav the Wise (1019-1054) Kiev had 400 churches, Europe's largest library east of Constantinople, and marriage alliances with France, Norway and Hungary.
rise: Viking princes (the Rus) sailing the river routes fused with Slavic trade towns: Oleg took Kiev in 882, and Rus' grew into a federation of principalities from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Vladimir the Great adopted Byzantine Christianity in 988 - the baptism that made Russia, Ukraine and Belarus Orthodox.
fall: The Mongols: Batu Khan's 1237-1240 campaign burned Vladimir, Kiev and a dozen cities - Kiev's Cathedral of the Tithes collapsed under refugees. The northeast principalities survived as Mongol tributaries, birthing Muscovy; the west turned to Lithuania and Poland.
legacy: The shared birth myth of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus; the Orthodox faith; and the word 'tsar' from Caesar.
quizFact: When Kiev fell to the Mongols in 1240, escaping refugees brought tales so dire that Europe feared 'the Tartars' were the apocalypse's army.
builder: Prince Oleg of Novgorod and the Rurikid dynasty that followed him.
reach: About 1.3 million km2 of river-linked forest and steppe from Ladoga to the Black Sea.
darkSide: The princely system ran on succession wars - brothers blinded cousins and burned their towns as routine policy (a blinded prince could not rule). Slavic and Turkic captives were exported down the rivers to Byzantine and Caspian slave markets for centuries.

name: Serbian Empire
peak: Stefan Dusan the Mighty ruled from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth - the most powerful Balkan state since Byzantium, with its own law code (Dusan's Code) and a crowned emperor.
rise: Rising as Byzantium weakened, Dusan conquered Macedonia, Albania, Epirus and Thessaly in 20 years, had himself crowned 'Emperor of Serbs and Greeks' in 1346, and was planning to take Constantinople itself.
fall: Dusan died suddenly (possibly poisoned) in 1355 mid-campaign. His empire split between feuding lords, and in 1371 the Ottoman army destroyed the Serbian nobility at the Maritsa river - the Ottoman doorstep into Europe.
legacy: Dusan's Code, Serbian medieval monasteries (UNESCO sites), and the memory of the empire that anchors Serbian national identity.
quizFact: Dusan's Code had 201 articles - including bans on bribery of judges and protections for villagers against raiding soldiers, 600 years ago.
builder: Stefan Dusan the Mighty of the Nemanjic dynasty.
reach: About 180,000 km2 across the central Balkans and northern Greece.
darkSide: Dusan's conquests depopulated Greek cities with deportations; his law code prescribed mutilation for bandits and burning for heretics. After his death, his half-brother and lords fought civil wars - and invited Ottoman troops as mercenaries, opening Europe's door to them.

name: Congo Free State
peak: King Leopold II's private possession - 2.3 million km2 run as one man's company, extracting rubber and ivory with an army of 19,000 African soldiers.
rise: Leopold II of Belgium grabbed the Congo basin under the guise of a humanitarian 'International African Association' at the 1884 Berlin Conference, and ran it as personal property - not a Belgian colony - until 1908.
fall: The Casement Report (1904) and missionary photographs of mutilated hands shocked the world; in 1908 even the Belgian parliament took it over. Estimates of the death toll from murder, famine, disease and collapsed birth rates range from 1 to 15 million.
legacy: The 20th century's first great human-rights campaign, Heart of Darkness, and a Congolese trauma that shaped its politics to today.
quizFact: Soldiers in Leopold's Congo had to present a severed hand per bullet used - proof they hadn't 'wasted' ammunition on hunting.
builder: Leopold II, King of the Belgians - as a private business venture disguised as philanthropy.
reach: The entire Congo basin, 76 times the size of Belgium.
darkSide: The rubber regime took hostages (usually women and children) against village quotas, cut hands and noses as punishment, and burned villages. Missionaries documented villages of one-handed adults. Populations in some regions fell by half - Leopold became rich while the world's first photo-atrocity campaign formed against him.
